title: Chicken Satay
subtitle: spiced chicken skewers with peanut dipping sauce
excerpt: Chicken satay is one of the most popular street foods across Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand. Marinated chicken is threaded onto skewers and grilled until charred. The peanut sauce is rich, slightly sweet, and tangy. Together they are one of the great combinations in South-East Asian cooking.
sourceNotes: Satay is believed to have originated in Java, Indonesia, inspired by Middle Eastern kebabs brought by Arab traders. It spread across South-East Asia and became a street food staple across the region. Malaysian satay is typically sweeter and more heavily spiced than Indonesian versions. It is served with compressed rice cakes (ketupat) and cucumber.

content.text: Satay is a street food that works perfectly at home. The marinade does most of the work -- give the chicken at least 30 minutes, longer if you can. The peanut sauce is made separately in a small pan and served warm alongside. A hot griddle or grill is essential to get the char that makes satay what it is.

items.prepNote: boneless, cut into long strips or 3cm chunks
use 4 tbsp peanut butter for the dipping sauce -- whisk with coconut milk, soy sauce, and lime juice
use coconut milk -- 200ml, for the peanut sauce
use soy sauce -- for the marinade and the peanut sauce

content.text: Make the marinade: mix the soy sauce, turmeric, cumin, garlic, ginger, brown sugar, and oil in a bowl.
Add the chicken strips and toss to coat. Marinate for at least 30 minutes, or overnight for deeper flavour.
Thread the chicken onto skewers (soak wooden skewers in water for 20 minutes first).
Make the peanut sauce: whisk the peanut butter with coconut milk, soy sauce, and lime juice in a small saucepan. Warm gently, stirring, until smooth. Add a little water to loosen if too thick.
Grill the satay on a hot griddle pan, under a grill, or over a barbecue for 3 to 4 minutes per side until charred at the edges and cooked through.
Serve immediately with the warm peanut sauce and sliced cucumber.

items.symptom: Peanut sauce is too thick and pasty
items.cause: Not enough liquid or peanut butter not properly combined
items.fix: Add warm water or coconut milk a tablespoon at a time, stirring over low heat, until it reaches a pourable consistency. The sauce should coat the back of a spoon.

content.text: Satay is a street food staple across Malaysia, Indonesia, and Singapore. In Kuala Lumpur, satay stalls serve until late at night. The peanut sauce is the essential partner -- its richness balances the char on the meat. Malaysian satay is typically served with compressed rice cakes (ketupat) and raw onion alongside.
